prompt:
An 83-year-old man in assisted living with type 2 diabetes, Parkinson disease, osteoporosis with a prior vertebral fracture, and stage 3b CKD has two months of intense itch and now tense blisters on his thighs, flexural arms, and lower abdomen covering about 30% of his body surface area. Biopsy shows a subepidermal blister with eosinophils, and direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane. Medications are linagliptin (started nine months ago), insulin glargine, carbidopa-levodopa, alendronate, and lisinopril. His A1c is 7.4%. Staff can apply creams, but he can't reach his back himself. His family is asking for pills to stop it fast. How should we treat him?

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Discontinue linagliptin because DPP-4 inhibitors are associated with bullous pemphigoid.
Adjust his diabetes regimen, such as titrating insulin, to replace linagliptin and monitor glucose.
Start whole-body superpotent topical corticosteroid such as clobetasol 0.05% cream applied to lesional and affected skin as first-line therapy.
Arrange for staff to apply the topical steroid with clear written instructions on quantity and sites.
Taper the topical corticosteroid gradually over several months according to disease control.
Consider doxycycline as a steroid-sparing adjunct.
Drain large tense blisters with a sterile needle while leaving the blister roof intact.
Use nonadherent dressings and emollients for eroded skin.
Monitor eroded areas for secondary infection.
Use a non-sedating antihistamine as an adjunct for itch if helpful.
If systemic corticosteroids become necessary, use the lowest effective dose with glucose monitoring, bone protection, and a planned taper.
Consider dupilumab or another steroid-sparing agent for disease refractory to topical therapy.
Obtain BP180 and BP230 antibody levels to support diagnosis and monitoring.
Arrange dermatology follow-up within two to four weeks.
Counsel the family that bullous pemphigoid is chronic and relapsing, not contagious, and may take months to remit.
Monitor for skin atrophy from prolonged topical corticosteroid use.
Monitor blood glucose more closely during extensive topical corticosteroid use because of systemic absorption.
Refer to dermatology for co-management.
Continue osteoporosis therapy and reassess fall and fracture risk if systemic steroids are needed.
Start prednisone 1 mg/kg daily as first-line therapy.
Continue linagliptin.
Switch linagliptin to another DPP-4 inhibitor such as sitagliptin.
Use only low-potency hydrocortisone cream.
Completely unroof blisters and remove the blister roof.
Start methotrexate without adjusting for his renal function.
Prescribe diphenhydramine or hydroxyzine for itch.
Use rituximab as first-line therapy.
Stop the topical corticosteroid abruptly once the blisters clear.
Prescribe empiric oral antibiotics for all blisters without signs of infection.
Start azathioprine without checking TPMT activity.
Treat the eruption as bullous impetigo with antibiotics alone.
Order routine whole-body CT screening for occult malignancy.
Stop all glucose-lowering therapy when linagliptin is stopped.
Apply adhesive tape or dressings directly to fragile skin.
Use intravenous immunoglobulin as first-line therapy.
Start dapsone without checking G6PD activity.
Prescribe a five-day oral steroid burst without a taper.
Repeat the skin biopsy because the diagnosis is uncertain.
